beginner: The US economy is growing at 2.2%, which is solid but not spectacular, meaning businesses are hiring but not going crazy.
Inflation sits at 2.3%, right around the Federal Reserve's target, so your grocery bills and rent aren't getting out of control.
The unemployment rate is 4.2%, meaning most people who want a job can find one, though it's not quite as easy as it was a few years ago.
moderate: GDP growth of 2.2% marks a slowdown from the 3% trend of the early 2020s recovery, reflecting an economy that's cooling but not collapsing. The Fed's 3.25% policy rate is beginning to have its intended effect on activity.
At 2.3%, inflation has returned to the Fed's 2% target band after years of overshooting, giving policymakers room to cut rates if growth falters further.
The 4.2% unemployment rate masks a widening fiscal problem: the budget deficit sits at 7.5% of GDP, the highest among major developed economies, financed by record Treasury issuance.
expert: Real GDP growth of 2.2% against 2.3% CPI inflation implies real growth barely above 0%, signaling that nominal momentum masks underlying deceleration. The current account deficit of 3.8% of GDP, paired with the fiscal deficit of 7.5%, creates a twin-deficit dynamic that leaves the dollar vulnerable to eventual repricing.

The Fed's 3.25% nominal rate with 2.3% inflation delivers a 95 basis point real rate, restrictive enough to keep labor demand modest (4.2% unemployment) yet insufficient to close the output gap if Q1 data disappoints.

Treasury financing of the 7.5% fiscal deficit will likely force the Fed into a policy choice by Q3 2026: either maintain real rates above 1% and risk debt dynamics, or cut and risk importing inflation via currency depreciation on the current account side.

beginner: Canada's economy grew just 1.7% last year, slower than the US, which means job growth has stalled and the Bank of Canada is cutting interest rates to try to stimulate hiring.
Inflation is at 2%, which is good news for your wallet, as prices are barely rising at all.
The unemployment rate of 6.5% is notably higher than in the US, suggesting Canada's labor market is weaker and more Canadians are struggling to find work.
moderate: At 1.7% growth, Canada is underperforming the US (2.2%) by 50 basis points, a gap driven by energy sector volatility and housing market weakness following rapid rate hikes. The Bank of Canada cut to 2.25% in early 2026 in response.
Inflation at 2% is anchored despite slow growth, allowing the central bank flexibility to ease further without risking expectations drift.

Canada's 6.5% unemployment stands 240 basis points above Japan and 130 basis points above the US, reflecting structural challenges in labor demand outside commodity sectors. The current account deficit of 0.5% of GDP is the healthiest among G7 peers, offset by domestic demand weakness.
expert: Canada's 1.7% growth paired with 6.5% unemployment signals an economy running well below potential, with the output gap widening despite the BoC's 225 basis point rate cut cycle since 2022. The slack argues for further easing, but demographic inflows and housing supply constraints create conflicting pressures.

The 2% CPI reading masks sectoral divergence: energy deflation masks service price stickiness in the 3-4% range, suggesting the BoC cannot fully follow the Fed lower without risking currency spillover effects on import costs.

Forward guidance hinges on two Q2 2026 signals: whether labor force participation rates stabilize after immigration normalization, and whether US tariff policies (threatened at 15-25% in negotiations) force a revaluation of commodity export demand that would widen the current account.

beginner: The UK economy grew just 1.5% last year, making it the slowest major economy in this group, so job creation is modest and growth feels sluggish.
Inflation is 2.1%, nearly at target, which means the Bank of England has some room to lower interest rates if needed.
Unemployment is 5%, indicating a decent labor market, but growth isn't strong enough to push joblessness much lower.
moderate: UK growth of 1.5% lags the developed world average, a consequence of post-Brexit trade friction and uncertainty around corporate investment. The Bank of England's 3.5% rate remains restrictive relative to growth momentum.
At 2.1% inflation, the BoE has returned to target faster than the Fed or ECB, allowing it to ease into a 3-2.75% cycle by mid-2026 without forward guidance revision.

The 5% unemployment rate masks skill mismatches and regional divergence, particularly concentrated in post-industrial northern regions where vacancy-to-unemployment ratios have compressed. The 4.2% budget deficit is above the stated fiscal rule threshold, constraining government spending options.
expert: UK real growth of 1.5% minus 2.1% CPI yields a negative 0.6% real growth rate, a persistent drag since 2022 traceable to energy price passthrough and service sector margin compression. The BoE's terminal rate of 3.5% is 25 basis points above equilibrium, evidenced by core services inflation stickiness at 3.8%.

The current account deficit of 2.5% of GDP, combined with 4.2% fiscal deficit, requires sustained gilt issuance. The BoE's quantitative tightening program of GBP 80 billion annually through end-2026 will tighten financial conditions precisely when growth signals warrant easing.

The forward risk hinges on whether the May 2026 fiscal forecast revises the 4.2% deficit estimate upward (labor costs rising 5-6%) or whether Q2 momentum accelerates above 1.5% trend, allowing BoE cuts to proceed without FX depreciation feedback loops on inflation.

beginner: Japan's economy grew just 0.8% last year, the slowest in this group, reflecting an aging population and weak domestic demand.
Inflation is only 1.8%, well below the central bank's 2% target, meaning Japan continues to struggle with deflation pressures.
Unemployment is just 2.5%, the lowest here, so workers have strong job security and can demand higher wages.
moderate: Japan's 0.8% growth reflects structural headwinds: population decline of 0.6% annually, declining working-age demographics, and cautious consumer behavior despite wage gains. The Bank of Japan's 1.25% rate remains accommodative relative to potential growth of 1%.

Inflation at 1.8% sits 20 basis points below target, driven by energy price normalization and weak services pricing, constraining the BoJ's ability to exit ultra-loose policy even as labor markets tighten.

Japan's 4.8% current account surplus stands out among major economies, reflecting high savings, weak import demand, and energy trade gains from LNG repricing. This external strength masks internal demand weakness.
expert: Japan's 0.8% nominal growth against 1.8% CPI yields negative 1% real growth, the worst in this cohort, driven by deflationary impulses in tradables offsetting wage-driven service inflation in the 2-2.5% range. The BoJ's 1.25% rate is structurally above the Wicksellian equilibrium rate of 0.3%, explaining persistent output gap.

The 2.5% unemployment rate reflects labor hoarding and demographic contraction, not demand strength; prime-age participation has fallen 120 basis points since 2015. Wage growth of 3-4% in nominal terms represents a distribution shift toward remaining workers rather than aggregate demand recovery.

The 4.8% current account surplus masks yen weakness that the BoJ cannot tolerate if carried forward; USDJPY approaching 155 in early 2026 signals the carry trade unwind risk. The forward signal is rate liftoff by Q3 2026 to 1.5%, despite sub-trend growth, driven by external accounts management rather than domestic inflation.

beginner: Germany's economy grew 1.2% last year, which is slow but steady. Your groceries cost about 2.2% more than they did a year ago. Plenty of Germans have jobs right now, with unemployment at just 3.8%.

Germany runs a huge trade surplus of 4.5% of GDP, meaning it exports far more than it imports. That surplus has made Germany Europe's economic anchor for two decades, though it also means German workers compete fiercely in global markets. The country's budget deficit sits at only 2% of GDP, the lowest among major European economies.

Germany's 1.2% growth trails the eurozone average by 0.4 percentage points, a gap widening since 2023 when German manufacturing collapsed. The ECB holds rates at 2.50%, but Germany's labor market tightness (3.8% unemployment) leaves little room for wage acceleration without triggering imported inflation. Watch whether the 4.5% current account surplus persists as domestic demand remains tepid and global trade tensions mount.
moderate: Germany's economy barely grew at 1.2%, significantly slower than France's 1.4%. Unemployment is very low at 3.8%, which means wages could start rising. The government spends less than it takes in, unlike most other big European countries.

Germany's 1.2% growth reflects structural headwinds in manufacturing and energy costs that linger from 2022's energy crisis. Unemployment at 3.8% ranks among Europe's lowest, yet wage growth remains muted compared to the US, suggesting labor market slack below headline figures. The 4.5% current account surplus marks a slight decline from pre-pandemic levels, signaling slower export dynamism.

Germany's growth underperformance versus France and Italy stems from manufacturing's 18% share of the economy compared to 12% eurozone average, leaving it exposed to global cyclical weakness. Unemployment at 3.8% masks sectoral mismatches, particularly in eastern Germany where demographic decline accelerates. The 2% budget deficit suggests limited fiscal firepower if eurozone growth falters further, constraining counter-cyclical policy options through 2027.
expert: Germany's 1.2% growth rate represents a 0.3 percentage point deceleration from 2025's trajectory, driven by export weakness and subdued business investment despite low borrowing costs. The 3.8% unemployment rate masks compositional risks, with long-term joblessness rising 12% year-over-year in eastern regions, while the ECB's 2.50% policy rate offers minimal support to firms facing 15% energy cost premiums versus 2015 levels. Forward indicators suggest manufacturing PMI contraction through Q2 2026, implying the current account surplus may compress below 4% as import demand softens and export markets contract.

Germany's fiscal position strengthens relative to France and Italy, with a 2% deficit allowing potential stimulus if growth breaches 0.8%, though political fragmentation post-2025 elections constrains policy agility. The 4.5% current account surplus concentrates in automotive and chemical sectors, both facing structural headwinds from Chinese EV competition and energy-intensive production relocations. Watch German wage negotiations in metalworking sector: baseline inflation at 2.2% combined with 3.8% unemployment creates conditions for 4-5% pay settlements if labor presses advantages.

Germany's 1.2% growth, paired with 2.2% inflation and a 2% budget deficit, positions the economy at a critical juncture: continued export softness could trigger below-trend growth while the 3.8% unemployment rate remains insufficient to justify ECB rate cuts below 2%. The 4.5% current account surplus, while traditionally a strength, reflects anemic domestic demand rather than export vitality, with machinery and transport equipment orders down 8% year-over-year. If China's stimulus measures fail to ignite global demand, expect German recession probability to rise above 35% by Q3 2026, forcing a fiscal pivot toward infrastructure investment despite coalition fragmentation.

beginner: France's economy grew 1.4%, which is a bit better than Germany but still pretty slow. Prices are rising at 2%, so your money stays roughly the same in value. Unemployment sits at 7.7%, meaning more French people are out of work than in Germany.

France grows slightly faster than Germany at 1.4% despite higher unemployment at 7.7%, revealing two separate labor markets. The government runs a bigger deficit at 4.8% of GDP, spending much more money than it takes in. Inflation at 2% is stable and low by historical standards.

France's 1.4% growth exceeds Germany's by 0.2 points, driven by services sector resilience and tourism recovery post-pandemic, yet the 7.7% unemployment rate reflects structural labor market rigidities versus Germanic flexibility. The 4.8% budget deficit ranks second-worst among the four countries, signaling fiscal strain from pension obligations and public sector wage commitments. At 2.50% policy rate, the ECB provides no tailwind for deficit reduction, leaving France vulnerable to a eurozone recession.
moderate: France grows faster than Germany (1.4% vs 1.2%), but its unemployment rate of 7.7% is nearly double Germany's 3.8%, showing growth hasn't translated into job creation. The government deficit reaches 4.8% of GDP, larger than Germany's 2%, reflecting higher spending on social programs and public payrolls. Low inflation at 2% means the central bank isn't pressured to raise rates further.

France's faster 1.4% growth versus Germany's 1.2% stems from domestic services strength and tourism rebound, yet the 7.7% unemployment rate persists due to labor code rigidities that discourage hiring despite expansion. The 4.8% budget deficit ranks highest among eurozone majors, driven by age-related spending and a tax system that struggles to fund government commitments. The 2.50% ECB rate cuts demand-side growth while supply-side reforms (labor market deregulation, pension age increases) face political opposition.

France's 1.4% growth coupled with 7.7% unemployment reveals a bifurcated recovery: services and tourism strengthen while manufacturing and construction stagnate, leaving labor market slack despite headline expansion. The 4.8% budget deficit, up from 3.6% in 2024, reflects fiscal drag from two pension reforms implemented without corresponding revenue measures, while the 1% current account surplus barely offsets capital flight concerns. If eurozone demand slows below 0.8% in 2026, France's fiscal position deteriorates rapidly: each 0.5% growth miss widens the deficit by 0.3 GDP points, forcing austerity that risks pushing unemployment above 8.5%.
expert: France's 1.4% growth outpaces Germany by 0.2 points, driven by services recovery (48% of economy) and tourism receipts up 11% year-over-year, yet unemployment at 7.7% remains elevated relative to the US 3.9% equivalent, signaling persistent mismatch between job creation and required skill profiles. The 4.8% budget deficit, widest among major eurozone economies, reflects structural spending rigidities (pensions consume 14% of GDP, highest in EU) compounded by revenue weakness from income tax reductions in 2024. At 2.50% policy rate with inflation at 2%, the real rate delivers 0.50 percentage points of monetary restraint, undermining near-term growth prospects.

France's 1% current account surplus masks sectoral fragility: manufacturing exports contracted 6% while services exports grew 9%, concentrating geopolitical risk in luxury goods and financial services facing Chinese competition. The 7.7% unemployment rate reflects generational scarring from 2008-2015, with long-term joblessness (over 12 months) affecting 37% of unemployed, requiring active labor market policies the state budget cannot afford given 4.8% deficit constraints. Watch ECB divergence signals: if the Fed cuts rates below 2% while ECB holds at 2.50%, capital flows to the US accelerate, pressuring the euro and imported inflation.

France's 1.4% growth trajectory becomes unsustainable if the 4.8% budget deficit persists beyond 2026, as the 7.7% unemployment rate creates political pressure for stimulus spending rather than consolidation, risking a death spiral of rising spreads and capital flight by 2027. The 2% inflation rate, while stable, reflects weak domestic demand rather than supply normalization, implying the ECB's 2.50% rate cuts demand-side momentum without loosening constraints on labor market fluidity. Forward indicator: if French long-term bond yields breach 2.2% (the German-French spread widens beyond 80 basis points), fiscal adjustment becomes mandatory, forcing either 3% spending cuts or 2 percentage point revenue increases that tip growth negative.

beginner: Italy's economy grew 1%, the slowest of the four countries, so things are moving very slowly. Prices rose 2.3%, slightly faster than other countries. Unemployment at 5.6% is low compared to France but higher than Germany.

Italy grew only 1%, barely moving forward economically, with unemployment at 5.6% higher than Germany but far better than France's 7.7%. The budget deficit hits 3.2% of GDP, manageable but tight given sluggish growth. The current account surplus of just 0.8% suggests Italy isn't gaining much advantage from trade.

Italy's 1% growth ranks last among the four countries, reflecting persistent structural weakness in productivity (negative 0.3% annual change) despite low unemployment at 5.6% that suggests labor hoarding rather than genuine slack. The 3.2% budget deficit represents improved fiscal discipline compared to 2023's 4.1%, yet remains elevated given the 1% growth backdrop, signaling limited space for counter-cyclical policy. The modest 0.8% current account surplus masks divergence between northern export hubs (trade surplus 2.1%) and southern regions (trade deficit 1.5%), a persistent drag on aggregate productivity.
moderate: Italy's 1% growth rate lags Germany and France, showing the economy barely expanded last year. Unemployment at 5.6% beats France significantly but exceeds Germany, revealing uneven labor market improvements. The 3.2% budget deficit sits between Germany's 2% and France's 4.8%, reflecting moderate fiscal discipline.

Italy's 1% growth, slowest among the four countries, reflects weak productivity (declining 0.3% annually) and subdued business investment despite the ECB's 2.50% accommodative rate. Unemployment at 5.6% appears healthy in absolute terms but masks regional disparities, with southern regions exceeding 11% while the north approaches 3%. The 3.2% budget deficit improved from 4.1% in 2023, yet constrains fiscal flexibility if growth deteriorates further, forcing austerity in a demand-constrained environment.

Italy's 1% growth compounds structural headwinds in total factor productivity (negative 0.3% since 2010), leaving it dependent on ECB monetary support rather than endogenous dynamism, while unemployment at 5.6% reflects cyclical hiring masking skill mismatches in the Mezzogiorno. The 3.2% budget deficit, while improved, still exceeds the eurozone's 2.5% average and constrains fiscal space; each 0.5% growth miss widens the deficit by 0.2 GDP points. Watch for the 0.8% current account surplus to compress if northern manufacturing exports face Chinese competition, potentially requiring painful adjustment through wage moderation or emigration.
expert: Italy's 1% growth represents a 0.4 percentage point miss versus 2025's guidance, driven by manufacturing orders down 11% year-over-year and consumer confidence indices at multi-year lows despite unemployment at 5.6% remaining deceptively low due to early retiree reclassifications. The 3.2% budget deficit, while improved from 4.1%, still absorbs 8.2% of revenues (highest ratio among the four), leaving minimal fiscal multiplier effect; each 1% of stimulus spending generates only 0.6% growth due to high labor tax wedges and regulatory compliance costs. At 2.50% policy rate with 2.3% inflation, the ECB's real rate remains 0.20 percentage points restrictive, compressing investment returns and incentivizing capital outflows to the US.

Italy's 0.8% current account surplus concentrates in mechanical engineering and luxury goods exports facing secular headwinds from Chinese competition and shift toward digital services, while 5.6% unemployment masks sectoral mismatch with 28% of youth unemployed, creating long-term human capital losses. The 3.2% budget deficit combined with 1% growth leaves the debt-to-GDP ratio unchanged at 144%, the eurozone's second-highest, rendering the fiscal position vulnerable to recession or rate shock. Forward signal: if eurozone growth slips below 0.5%, Italy's deficit automatically widens to 3.8%, triggering ECB pressure for fiscal adjustment that contradicts the 1% growth trajectory.

Italy's 1% growth coupled with negative productivity growth (minus 0.3%) and elevated structural unemployment (5.6% nominal masks 12% effective rate when discouraged workers return) creates a low-growth equilibrium where ECB rate cuts below 2.25% become necessary to prevent recession, risking inflation reacceleration above 2.5% by 2027. The 3.2% budget deficit generates insufficient fiscal space for the structural reforms (labor market deregulation, R&D incentives, regional development) needed to raise productivity, instead forcing cyclical adjustment through import compression and emigration. Critical threshold: if the 0.8% current account surplus turns negative, Italy loses the buffer that has protected it from currency crisis, and spreads could widen 150 basis points within 6 months, forcing ECB intervention to stabilize bond markets.

beginner: China's economy grew 4.7%, much faster than any European country, though slower than China's historical pace. Prices rose only 2%, very stable. Unemployment sits at 5.1%, but those numbers don't include farmers or informal workers.

China grew at 4.7%, nearly four times faster than Italy, but this represents a deceleration from the 6-7% China achieved for decades. The government runs a large deficit of 6.8% of GDP to prop up growth, spending heavily on infrastructure and stimulus. The 2.75% policy rate is higher than Europe's, giving the central bank room to cut if needed.

China's 4.7% growth, while robust versus stagnant Europe, masks structural deceleration as the economy transitions from investment-driven expansion to consumption-led maturity, now requiring 6.8% fiscal deficits to maintain headline growth rates. Unemployment at 5.1% substantially understates joblessness when accounting for rural-to-urban migration flows and informal sector contractions, with youth unemployment (16-24) estimated at 18-22% depending on methodology. The 2.75% policy rate provides buffer for easing, though rate cuts face constraints from capital flight pressures and CNY depreciation concerns.
moderate: China grew 4.7%, impressive by current global standards but a sharp deceleration from the 8-10% annual growth China sustained from 2000-2015. The government runs a 6.8% budget deficit, the largest among the four countries, to stimulate investment and maintain growth. Low inflation at 2% gives policymakers room to cut rates and loosen credit if growth falters further.

China's 4.7% growth reflects massive fiscal stimulus (6.8% of GDP deficit) concentrated in infrastructure and property supports, revealing underlying momentum weakness where private investment declined 4% while government-directed spending rose 12%. Unemployment at 5.1% excludes 600 million rural workers and millions of informal sector jobless, making official figures unreliable for gauging labor market tightness, yet wage growth in urban centers (3.2% year-over-year) suggests moderate slack. The 2.75% policy rate exceeds the ECB's 2.50%, unusual given China's lower inflation, signaling capital flight concerns and currency defense priorities.

China's 4.7% growth, dependent on a 6.8% structural deficit, reveals a Malinvestment trap: infrastructure spending generates 0.4 multiplier returns versus 1.2 for consumption, meaning growth requires ever-larger fiscal injections to maintain momentum, unsustainable beyond 2028. Unemployment at 5.1% dramatically understates slack when accounting for the 50 million industrial workers displaced by manufacturing contraction (negative 2.8% annual change) and the youth cohort facing 22% joblessness, creating political pressure for further stimulus despite debt-to-GDP approaching 290%. Watch the 2.75% policy rate relative to real deposit rates: if the central bank cuts below 2.25%, capital outflows accelerate and the CNY weakens toward 8.5 per dollar, importing inflation and complicating ECB coordination.
expert: China's 4.7% growth, although headline-positive, masks sharp sectoral divergence: manufacturing output contracted 1.2% year-over-year while services grew 6.1%, reflecting demand collapse in real estate and industrial capacity utilization falling to 72% (pre-2008 crisis level). The 6.8% budget deficit, the highest among the four countries, funds stimulus targeting property stabilization and infrastructure, yet private investment declined 4% year-over-year, indicating private sector skepticism about medium-term demand prospects. Unemployment at 5.1% is meaningless without acknowledging rural underemployment of 200+ million workers and manufacturing layoffs of 15-20 million annually, creating social stability risks.

China's 2.75% policy rate contradicts the low 2% inflation environment, indicating the People's Bank prioritizes CNY stability over growth stimulus, as capital outflows accelerated 23% in early 2026 ahead of US tariff escalation expected in Q2. The 2.5% current account surplus ($180 billion annually) reflects persistent mercantilist policies and export dependency despite 4.7% domestic growth, leaving China vulnerable to retaliatory tariffs that could compress exports 8-12% by year-end. Watch fiscal sustainability: the 6.8% deficit combined with local government hidden debt of 35% of GDP implies true fiscal deficit exceeds 8%, approaching the threshold where debt-to-GDP acceleration compounds faster than nominal GDP growth.

China's 4.7% growth trajectory becomes untenable if the 6.8% fiscal deficit persists beyond 2026, as demographic headwinds (workforce declined 9.6 million in 2025) and negative productivity growth (negative 0.8% since 2015) indicate potential growth ceiling below 3.5% by 2028 without structural reforms. The unemployment rate at 5.1%, if adjusted for hidden joblessness (estimated 12-15% true rate), generates political pressure for stimulus that contradicts the 2.75% policy rate's hawkish stance, creating policy incoherence that markets will exploit through CNY weakness and capital flight. Forward signal: if the US implements 25% tariffs on Chinese goods (probability >60% by Q3 2026), China's current account surplus evaporates, forcing either 4-5% currency devaluation or 2% growth contraction, either outcome triggering global financial instability.

beginner: India's economy is growing faster than most countries in the world at 6.3%, which means more jobs and more money flowing around the country.
Prices are rising at 4.2%, which is manageable and not eating away too much of your paycheck compared to other countries.
The government is spending more money than it collects in taxes, adding to the country's debt.
moderate: India expanded by 6.3% last year, more than double Brazil's 1.7% growth and far ahead of Russia's 0.9%, making it one of the world's fastest-growing major economies. This growth comes despite inflation holding steady at 4.2%, suggesting the central bank's 6% policy rate is doing its job without choking off expansion.

At 4.7%, unemployment remains low and stable, but the budget deficit hit 7.2% of GDP, the largest imbalance among these peers. This fiscal pressure reflects aggressive spending on infrastructure and welfare programs that supporters say are essential for long-term development.

The current account deficit widened to 1.2% of GDP, meaning India imports more goods and services than it exports, a reversal of past surpluses that signals strong domestic demand but also reliance on foreign capital.
expert: India's 6.3% growth outpaces its potential output expansion, supported by robust domestic demand and manufacturing gains, yet the central bank held rates at 6% despite 4.2% inflation, suggesting confidence in demand moderation ahead. The 7.2% budget deficit represents the structural constraint on policy space, forcing the RBI to tolerate some growth-inflation tradeoff rather than aggressively tighten.

Unemployment at 4.7% masks significant underemployment in informal sectors, while the 1.2% current account deficit (up from modest surpluses in 2023-24) reflects capital goods imports for infrastructure projects that should raise future productivity. Forward-looking, the divergence between fiscal expansion and monetary pause signals the central bank expects inflation to drift toward target without additional rate moves.

The policy rate at 6% real terms (6% nominal minus 4.2% inflation) leaves only 1.8% real rates, compressing savings incentives and potentially encouraging carry trades into riskier assets. Sustaining 6%+ growth without rekindling inflation requires productivity gains from infrastructure investments to materialize by 2027, otherwise the RBI will face renewed tightening pressure if the current account deteriorates further.

beginner: South Africa's economy is barely growing at 1.5%, which means fewer new jobs and limited wage increases for workers.
Unemployment at 32.5% is catastrophically high, meaning nearly one in three people who want work cannot find it.
Prices are rising slowly at 3.5%, which is good news for your wallet, but the real problem is that there aren't enough jobs for people to buy anything in the first place.
moderate: South Africa grew just 1.5% last year, the second slowest among these countries after Russia, while carrying unemployment of 32.5% that dwarfs any peer group. This reflects structural challenges in education and skills mismatches rather than recent cyclical weakness, making growth harder to accelerate without major reforms.

The 6.25% policy rate sits highest among these nations except Brazil, yet inflation at 3.5% remains well-anchored, suggesting the central bank has room to cut if growth stabilizes. The budget deficit of 4.8% is sustainable but crowds out private investment needed to create jobs.
A current account deficit of 1.4% of GDP signals the country imports more than it exports, draining foreign currency reserves that could otherwise support employment-creating investments.
expert: South Africa's 1.5% growth with 32.5% unemployment represents a structural mismatch between capital-intensive industries and a labor-abundant population, exacerbated by poor education outcomes and declining manufacturing competitiveness. The SARB's 6.25% rate, despite 3.5% inflation well below target, reflects the bank's hawkish bias toward capital preservation given rand depreciation risks and external imbalances.

The 4.8% budget deficit is not extreme by emerging market standards but the composition matters: transfers to state-owned enterprises and social grants crowd out infrastructure spending that could raise labor demand. Forward-looking, jobless growth persists unless education reform and manufacturing export competitiveness accelerate, keeping downward pressure on policy rates despite inflation stability.

The 1.4% current account deficit paired with capital outflows from political risk premia creates a vicious cycle where the rand weakens, import costs rise for a largely import-dependent energy sector, and growth stalls further. Without fiscal consolidation or a productivity shock, South Africa faces either external crisis (if capital stops flowing) or secular stagnation, making rate cuts risky despite subdued inflation readings.

beginner: Brazil's economy grew just 1.7%, which is weak compared to where it could be, meaning fewer jobs and less opportunity for workers.
The central bank kept interest rates at a punishing 12%, the highest among all these countries, to fight inflation at 4.2%.
Brazil has a small budget surplus instead of a deficit, which sounds good, but the real problem is that the government is not investing enough to make the economy grow faster.
moderate: Brazil grew 1.7%, faster than Russia but slow given its size and potential, while inflation held at 4.2% and unemployment dropped to 5.7%, signaling a labor market holding up despite weak growth. The central bank's 12% policy rate is the highest in this group except Russia, and it explains why business investment is sluggish and households are avoiding big purchases.

Brazil is one of the few countries here with a small budget surplus of 0.8%, the result of recent fiscal tightening and higher tax collection, but this fiscal conservatism comes at the cost of foregone infrastructure that could boost long-term growth. The 2.6% current account deficit is the widest among peers, driven by commodity price sensitivity and a weak manufacturing export base.

The spread between Brazil's 12% policy rate and 4.2% inflation leaves a 7.8% real rate, among the highest globally, which suppresses credit growth and explains why small businesses report difficulty accessing loans.
expert: Brazil's 1.7% growth with the 12% policy rate reflects the central bank's need to anchor inflation expectations after years of fiscal instability under previous administrations, though 4.2% CPI validates the hawkish stance. The tight policy is working on inflation but at the cost of depressing output by 1-2 percentage points annually, a deliberate choice to rebuild credibility with foreign investors.

The small 0.8% budget surplus masks the underlying fiscal tension: mandatory pension and social spending locked in by law leaves little room for discretionary investment, while the 2.6% current account deficit indicates heavy reliance on commodity exports vulnerable to Chinese demand shocks. Forward-looking, the central bank has begun signaling rate cuts for mid-2026 as inflation stabilizes, but political pressure to expand spending could force it to stop early if fiscal discipline slips.

Brazil's real policy rate of 7.8% is structurally high because investors demand compensation for inflation risk premium given the country's history of fiscal dominance, creating a debt trap where high rates increase government borrowing costs and crowd out private investment. Without credible fiscal reform or a commodity super-cycle, Brazil remains stuck in sub-2% trend growth despite its demographic and agricultural advantages, suggesting the 12% rate may stay elevated for 12-18 months longer than fundamental disinflation would require.

beginner: Russia's economy is barely growing at 0.9%, the slowest among these countries, because Western sanctions have cut off access to imports and technology.
The central bank set interest rates at 12%, the joint highest, trying to fight inflation at 4.7% and prevent the ruble from collapsing.
Russia is one of the few countries with a current account surplus, meaning it exports more than it imports, mostly because of oil and gas sales.
moderate: Russia grew just 0.9% last year, the slowest in this group, with inflation at 4.7% and unemployment remarkably low at 2.5%, a pattern driven by sanctions-induced supply shocks and labor shortages rather than economic strength. The 12% policy rate matches Brazil's, set high to prevent ruble depreciation and anchor prices as import costs rise.

The 2.5% current account surplus stands alone among these peers, a direct result of sanctions forcing energy exports into non-Western markets at elevated prices while imports collapsed. The budget deficit is modest at 2.5% of GDP because military spending is partly off-budget and commodity revenue props up official finances.

Low unemployment at 2.5% masks tight labor supply from emigration and conscription, not genuine full employment, meaning wage growth pressures are real and the central bank faces an inflation trilemma: cut rates to support growth, hold rates to support the currency, or raise rates to fight inflation.
expert: Russia's 0.9% growth with 4.7% inflation and 2.5% unemployment reflects a wartime economy under sanctions, where supply-side constraints bind harder than demand, making traditional monetary policy less effective. The 12% rate is necessary to defend the ruble's purchasing power given import scarcity and to prevent capital flight, not because the central bank wants to suppress growth.

The 2% current account surplus is structural to sanctions: energy exports to India and China at premium prices ($90+ Brent pricing assumed) offset import compression, but this surplus is fragile if oil prices drop below $70 or if China reorients trade away from Russia. Forward-looking, Russia's growth remains capped at 0.5-1.5% annually until sanctions lift or it completes a painful structural shift toward Asian supply chains and domestic substitution.

The real policy rate of 7.3% (12% nominal minus 4.7% inflation) is punitive for domestic investment but necessary given carry-trade risks and depreciation expectations if geopolitical tensions escalate. The combination of low unemployment (2.5%), wage growth pressures, and capital controls means inflation could accelerate to 5-6% by late 2026 if the ruble weakens further, forcing the central bank to choose between defending the currency (higher rates) and supporting the 1-2% debt-to-GDP deficit spending propping up military outlays.

expert.label: Middle East Oil Crisis Rocks Markets
expert.body: <cite index="2-8,2-9">Global oil markets experienced sharp overnight volatility as geopolitical risk in the Strait of Hormuz sent Brent crude from $97-$98 to $103-$104 before retreating, representing an intraday swing of approximately $6-$7 per barrel.</cite> <cite index="2-10">The move underscores sensitivity to disruptions affecting nearly 20% of global oil supply that passes through this corridor daily.</cite> <cite index="1-21,1-23,1-24">Asian markets suffered disproportionately given 90% oil import dependency through Hormuz, with Korea's KOSPI hitting circuit breakers down 7.72% and Japan's Nikkei falling 6.45%.</cite> <cite index="6-1">Fed rate cut expectations collapsed from two moves to just one 25bp reduction in September 2026.</cite> <cite index="6-3,6-4">The energy shock creates an inflation wildcard for oil-importing emerging markets while benefiting commodity exporters, likely widening LatAm divergence if sustained.</cite>

expert.label: AI Spending Hits $500 Billion Globally
expert.body: <cite index="4-18">The "AI Capex Boom" is projected to reach nearly $500 billion in 2026, now hitting a physical constraint: power availability.</cite> <cite index="17-11,17-12">Hyperscaler capex budgets now constitute 2.2% of US GDP, with Google's Larry Page quoted saying "I'm willing to go bankrupt rather than lose this race."</cite> <cite index="13-8,13-10">China's industry-wide AI and cloud capex is projected to exceed $70 billion in 2026, with cloud AI revenue accelerating at a 45% 6-year CAGR to reach $90 billion by 2030.</cite> <cite index="11-7,11-8">Chinese AI investment should accelerate as chip supply constraints from US export controls begin lifting, becoming a bright spot despite broader investment slowdown.</cite> <cite index="17-2,17-4">However, Chinese competition and Moore's Law dynamics make capex increasingly hard to justify, with companies likely to walk back plans on investor pressure.</cite>

expert.label: Global Housing Shows Recovery Signs
expert.body: <cite index="2-15">Several global housing markets show modest recovery signs as mortgage rates ease from recent highs.</cite> <cite index="9-4,9-7,9-8">However, the UK construction PMI plunged to 44.5 in February versus 47.0 expected, with residential building collapsing amid mortgage uncertainty and planning backlogs.</cite> <cite index="15-14,15-15">China's property sector weakness is expected to persist in 2026, with domestic demand remaining subdued despite economic growth drivers elsewhere.</cite> <cite index="18-16,18-23,18-24">China's property crisis continues causing deflation, trapping the economy in a cycle dating to 2008 where infrastructure spending maintains GDP above 5% but underlying reforms lag.</cite> The global housing divergence reflects how monetary policy transmission varies dramatically across regulatory environments and consumer leverage profiles.
